overview.text: Founded on February 12, 1909, after years of racial violence and the 1908 Springfield race riot, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) brought together Black leaders and white reformers to oppose racial discrimination and secure constitutional rights. The organization pursued change through legal challenges, public advocacy, local branches, and journalism. In 1910, W.E.B. Du Bois became its director of publications and research and edited The Crisis, the NAACP’s magazine, which covered civil rights and Black life and culture. The NAACP’s sustained legal campaign against school segregation helped bring cases before the Supreme Court; in 1954, Brown v. Board of Education ruled public-school segregation unconstitutional.

key_facts.text: The NAACP was founded in 1909; its founding call followed the 1908 Springfield race riot and was signed by Black and white participants.
Early aims included opposing lynching and racial injustice and securing rights protected by the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments.
The NAACP launched The Crisis in 1910, with W.E.B. Du Bois as editor; the magazine reported on the organization and covered race, politics, and Black culture.
The NAACP’s legal campaign challenged school segregation over many years and contributed to the cases leading to Brown v. Board of Education.
On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court ruled that racial segregation in public schools violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause.
